claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of treatment response variability.

claims.claim: Poor cell survival in implants correlates with lack of hypoglycemic effect in STZ mice.
claims.source: Although a portion of animals (~25% of experimental mice) did not show an appreciable hypoglycemic effect, it was revealed at the end of the experiment that cells in the implants survived poorly in these mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that non-responders had poor cell survival.

claims.claim: Average plasma insulin levels in cell-implanted STZ mice are higher than levels in sham controls.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by plasma insulin measurements (Figure 5e).

claims.claim: Plasma insulin levels in cell-implanted STZ mice are still much below the levels of normal mice.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5e, average plasma insulin levels in cell-implanted STZ mice were in general higher than the levels in sham controls, although they were still much below the reference of normal mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by plasma insulin measurements (Figure 5e).

claims.claim: Hypothalamic islet implantation does not induce regeneration of pancreatic islets in STZ mice.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pancreatic histology analysis (Figure 5f,g).

claims.claim: Mouse survival rate remarkably increased by hypothalamic islet implantation in STZ diabetes model.
claims.source: Our results showed that mouse survival rate remarkably increased by this treatment (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve analysis (Figure 6a).

claims.claim: The majority of death in sham-operated STZ mice occurred within 40 days after STZ injection.
claims.source: While the majority of death occurred within 40 days after STZ injection in the sham group, death was greatly avoided when htNSCPGHM islets were implanted.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data (Figure 6a).

claims.claim: Death was greatly avoided when hypothalamic islets were implanted in STZ mice.
claims.source: While the majority of death occurred within 40 days after STZ injection in the sham group, death was greatly avoided when htNSCPGHM islets were implanted.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data (Figure 6a).

claims.claim: Hypothalamic islet implantation improved body weight in STZ mice.
claims.source: Improvement of general health by this treatment was also reflected by improved body weight (Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements (Figure 6b).

claims.claim: There is a lack of correlation between hyperglycemia and survival in sham STZ mice.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6c, there was a lack of correlation between hyperglycemia and survival in sham STZ model, suggesting that death of STZ mice was not simply a result of hyperglycemia when blood glucose levels were very high.

claims.claim: Death of STZ mice is not simply a result of hyperglycemia when blood glucose levels are very high.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6c, there was a lack of correlation between hyperglycemia and survival in sham STZ model, suggesting that death of STZ mice was not simply a result of hyperglycemia when blood glucose levels were very high.

claims.claim: There is only a tendency of relationship between blood glucose and survival in sphere-treated STZ mice.

claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the weak correlation between blood glucose reduction and survival improvement.

claims.claim: There is a lack of clear correlation between blood insulin level and survival in sham STZ mice.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6e).

claims.claim: The correlation between insulin and survival is marginally significant in sphere-treated STZ mice.

claims.claim: Elevation in blood insulin could have a partial contribution to the improved survival of sphere-treated STZ mice.

results.result: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells (htNSCs) produce multiple pancreatic (insulin, glucagon, somatostatin), gastrointestinal (galanin, VIP, CCK, PACAP), and hypothalamic peptides (NPY, AgRP, α-MSH, CRF, GnRH, oxytocin) in subcellular vesicles, with subpopulations co-expressing multiple peptides.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C15, C24-C27 are well-supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplements 1-2, 5), qPCR data, and vesicle marker co-localization studies showing differential localization of peptides in LDCV vs. SLMV. The evidence converges to demonstrate multifaceted peptide production by htNSCs.

results.result: Approximately 7%, 2%, and 3% of htNSCs show insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin promoter activity respectively, with substantial overlap: ~25% of insulin-promoter-active cells co-activate somatostatin promoter, ~20% co-activate glucagon promoter, and ~44% of glucagon-promoter-active cells co-activate somatostatin promoter.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are supported by Flp recombinase reporter assays (Figure 1c) and dual Flp/Cre reporter system data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The quantitative measurements provide clear evidence for the percentages and overlap of promoter activities.

results.result: Insulin promoter-selected htNSCs can be isolated via FACS and secrete insulin in a glucose-regulated manner, with ~3-fold increase at high glucose (20 mM) vs. low glucose (2 mM), and respond to KCl and arginine stimulation. This insulin-secreting activity is preserved over at least 10 passages.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C28-C33 are supported by FACS data (Figure 1e), luminescent reporter assays (Figure 2a), and ELISA measurements (Figure 2b,c) showing glucose-dependent and stimulation-responsive insulin secretion. The data demonstrate successful isolation and functional characterization of insulin-secreting htNSCs.

results.result: 3D spheroid culture of insulin promoter-selected htNSCs increases insulin secretion >30-fold compared to monolayer culture. These spheres secrete insulin, somatostatin, glucagon, VIP, CCK, and PACAP, showing similar glucose-response patterns to pancreatic islets but with much lower insulin secretion capacity per cell.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C42 are supported by comparing ELISA measurements between monolayer (Figure 2b) and sphere cultures (Figure 2d-i). The substantial increase in insulin secretion in 3D culture and the secretion of multiple peptides are well-documented, though the lower capacity compared to islets is acknowledged.

results.result: Insulin promoter-selected htNSC spheres express pancreatic islet biomarkers (PC1/3, GLUT2, KIR6.2, NKX2.2) and contain higher percentages of somatostatin-positive cells than pancreatic islets, with somatostatin-positive cells distributed peripherally. Unlike pancreatic islets, these spheres strongly express NSC biomarkers Sox2 and nestin.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 are supported by comprehensive immunostaining data (Figure 3a-b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1-2) comparing htNSC spheres to pancreatic islets. The data demonstrate that these spheres have combined features of pancreatic islets and neural stem cells.

results.result: Somatostatin- and glucagon-positive cells are crucial for sphere formation: when either is depleted, remaining cells fail to form spheres despite presence of insulin-positive cells. However, when insulin-positive cells are depleted, remaining cells can still form spheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by cell ablation experiments using promoter-driven DTR (Figure 3c). The differential requirement for different cell types in sphere formation is clearly demonstrated, though the underlying mechanism is not fully elucidated.

results.result: Hypothalamic islet spheres strongly express exosomal biomarkers CD81 and TSG101 in >90% of cells and secrete considerably high amounts of exosomal miRNAs, while pancreatic islets barely express these markers or secrete exosomal miRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by immunostaining quantification (Figure 4a-b) and small RNA bio-analyzer assays (Figure 4c-d). The stark contrast between htNSC spheres and pancreatic islets in exosome production is well-documented.

results.result: Peripheral implantation of htNSC spheres in the great omentum of STZ mice results in ~50% cell survival over 1 month, with fasting blood glucose dropping below 300 mg/dL in the majority of mice shortly after implantation. Effects remain for weeks, though ~25% of mice show poor response correlated with poor cell survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 are supported by cell survival analysis (Figure 5b,c) and blood glucose measurements (Figure 5d). The moderate antidiabetic effect and variability in response are clearly documented, with appropriate correlation to implant survival.

results.result: Cell-implanted STZ mice show higher plasma insulin levels than sham controls but still much below normal mice. The treatment does not induce pancreatic islet regeneration, as pancreatic damage is similar between implanted and sham groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by plasma insulin measurements (Figure 5e) and pancreatic histology analysis (Figure 5f,g). The data clearly demonstrate that the therapeutic effect is from the implanted cells, not from pancreatic regeneration.

results.result: Peripheral implantation of hypothalamic islet spheres in STZ mice leads to remarkable improvements in survival (majority of sham deaths occur within 40 days, greatly avoided with implantation), body weight, muscle strength, treadmill running capability, and voluntary locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C69-C72, C80-C82 are supported by survival curve analysis (Figure 6a), body weight measurements (Figure 6b), and behavioral tests (Figure 6g-i). The pro-survival and health-improving effects are dramatic and well-documented across multiple outcome measures.

results.result: The pro-survival and metabolic effects of hypothalamic islet spheres are dissociable: there is lack of correlation between hyperglycemia and survival in sham STZ mice, and only a tendency of relationship in sphere-treated mice. Blood insulin shows marginally significant correlation with survival in treated mice, suggesting partial contribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C73-C79 are supported by correlation analyses (Figure 6c-f). The statistical analyses demonstrate that survival benefits are not simply explained by glucose lowering, though the correlations are weak and the mechanistic basis requires further investigation.

results.result: Production of insulin by hypothalamic islet spheres is important for the antidiabetic effect: insulin knockdown completely abrogates glucose-lowering effects, indicating that elevated plasma insulin from implanted spheres accounts for the moderate hypoglycemic effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C83-C84 are supported by blood glucose measurements in insulin-knockdown groups (Figure 7a,b). The complete loss of glucose-lowering effect with insulin knockdown provides strong evidence for insulin's role in the metabolic benefit.

results.result: Secretion of exosomes by hypothalamic islet spheres is essential for enhancing survival: Rab27a knockdown (inhibiting exosome secretion) completely abrogates survival benefits and behavioral improvements without affecting glucose-lowering. Conversely, insulin-knockdown spheres retain dramatic survival benefits despite loss of glucose control.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C85-C89 are supported by survival curves (Figure 7c) and behavioral tests (Figure 7d-g) comparing insulin-knockdown vs. exosome-inhibited spheres. The differential effects clearly demonstrate that exosomes mediate survival benefits independently of glucose control.

results.result: Hypothalamic islet spheres have differential roles in improving metabolic physiology versus general health, with multifaceted secretion (insulin for glucose control, exosomes for survival) mechanistically important for different therapeutic aspects.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are well-supported by the comprehensive knockdown experiments (Figure 7) showing that insulin and exosomes mediate distinct therapeutic effects. This represents a key mechanistic insight of the study.

results.result: Co-existence of pancreatic hormones in the same cells can be seen in some immature islets of Langerhans, suggesting a developmental relationship between htNSCs and pancreatic islet precursors.
results.evaluation: Claim C22 is supported by citations to published literature, but claim C23 is speculative inference from similarity in co-expression patterns. The developmental relationship is suggested but not directly demonstrated in this study.

results.result: Background context: The hypothalamus is a major site of insulin expression outside pancreatic islets, contains Sox2-positive neural stem cells capable of three-lineage differentiation, has limited neurogenic activity in adult rodents, and htNSCs have endocrine functions through exosome secretion contributing to aging control.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C99 are supported by citations to established literature and prior work by the authors. These provide appropriate background context for the current study.

results.result: The authors suggest that diabetic management should consider health-enhancing endocrine factors beyond glucose control, that the therapy might be more effective in milder diabetes, and that their findings might explain FGF treatment effects on diabetes remission.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are speculative suggestions and extrapolations from the current findings. While reasonable hypotheses, they lack direct experimental support and represent future directions rather than established results.

results.result: Hypothalamic neural stem cells contain tanycytes that proliferate in response to FGF stimulation, and FGF is important for maintaining and growing hypothalamic spheres in this study.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is supported by citation to published literature, and claim C104 is based on observations during sphere culture. These provide relevant methodological and contextual information.
